steps.body: When the numerator matches the denominator, you are holding every piece the whole was cut into — so 5/5, 8/8, and 3/3 all equal 1.

widget.prompt: Build a fraction that equals exactly one whole using sixths.
widget.successFeedback: 6/6 — every one of the six pieces, which together are the whole.
widget.lowFeedback: Your shaded amount is less than the target 6/6. Compare it with the target, then increase the shaded amount.
widget.highFeedback: Your shaded amount is greater than the target 6/6. Compare it with the target, then decrease the shaded amount.

commonFractions.feedback: 5/6 leaves one piece unshaded — just short of the whole.
1/6 is a single piece of six, far from the complete whole.

predict.reveal: Seven of the seven pieces is all of them — the whole, rebuilt exactly.

cml.actionGoal: Cut, count, and compare equal pieces to see what g3f equal one really names.
invariants: A fraction names equal shares of ONE whole: the denominator says how many equal pieces the whole became, and the numerator counts them, which is what makes g3f equal one comparable at all.
misconceptions: Calling unequal pieces fractions, reading the denominator as a count, or comparing fractions that came from different-sized wholes.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: If the whole changed size, which of these comparisons would stop being trustworthy?

widget.prompt: Convert 8/8 to a mixed number. What is the WHOLE NUMBER part?

commonErrors.feedback: 8 is how many PIECES there are; all 8 of them together rebuild exactly one whole.
8/8 is not less than a whole — it is every piece the whole was cut into.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Name the equal pieces the whole was cut into, then count how many of them the question is about.
